pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Effects of Drugs & Alcohol

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Health):** "the effects of recreational drugs (including substance misuse) on behaviour, health and life processes."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No specific MS performance expectation; substance-effect content is handled in US health education rather than NGSS science. This is UK-led. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children classify common recreational drugs by their effect on the nervous system — depressants (slow it, e.g. alcohol), stimulants (speed it up, e.g. nicotine, caffeine) and hallucinogens (distort perception) — and explain specific effects of alcohol (liver damage, impaired judgement/reactions) and tobacco (lung disease, cancer, cardiovascular harm). They distinguish physical dependence (the body adapts and needs the drug) from psychological dependence (craving), and connect drug effects to the body systems they act on. The move that matters is mechanistic and non-moralising: a drug is a chemical that changes how a body SYSTEM works, with short-term behavioural effects and long-term health consequences.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). Extends KS2 'diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle affect the body'; a mature health topic. A child is secure when they can classify a drug as depressant/stimulant/hallucinogen, name a specific organ effect of alcohol and of tobacco, and distinguish physical from psychological dependence.
bestPractices: Frame drugs mechanistically and non-judgementally — a chemical that changes how a body system works — rather than moralising, which improves both accuracy and engagement.
Anchor classification (depressant/stimulant/hallucinogen) to the nervous-system effect, then attach specific organ harms for alcohol and tobacco.
Separate physical from psychological dependence explicitly, as pupils routinely conflate them.
Use accurate, age-appropriate, non-sensational information and attend to safeguarding and pupils' personal contexts.
Connect effects to the body systems already studied (nervous, circulatory, respiratory, liver) so it consolidates prior learning.
keyRepresentations: Body-map of organ-specific effects (liver, lungs, brain, heart)
Depressant / stimulant / hallucinogen classification chart tied to nervous-system effect
Reaction-time / behaviour change illustration for depressants vs stimulants
commonMisconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant because it can make people lively — it is a depressant.
Believing dependence is only physical (missing psychological dependence/craving).
Assuming legal drugs (alcohol, tobacco) are therefore harmless.
Thinking harm is only immediate, missing long-term/cumulative organ damage.
Treating all illegal drugs as identical rather than having different classes and effects.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 13–14) study how recreational drugs act on the body as chemicals that change how a body SYSTEM works — framed mechanistically and non-judgementally. Core tasks: classify drugs as depressants (slow the nervous system, e.g. alcohol), stimulants (speed it up, e.g. nicotine, caffeine) or hallucinogens (distort perception); attach specific organ harms to alcohol (liver damage/cirrhosis, impaired judgement and reactions) and tobacco (lung disease and cancer, cardiovascular harm); and distinguish physical dependence (body adapts, withdrawal) from psychological dependence (craving/compulsion). A body-map reveal activity, a probing in-role dialogue, a classification check, and an optional reaction-time model each address different facets. All content must be age-appropriate, non-sensational and safeguarding-aware.

activities.title: Tappable body-map of drug effects with myth-busting flaps
feedback: If a learner classes alcohol as a stimulant from the initial 'confidence', the flap corrects: early disinhibition comes from depressing self-control, but overall alcohol slows the nervous system, so it is a depressant — point to its effect on reaction times.
If a learner thinks 'depressant' means 'makes you sad', clarify that here it means it slows (depresses) nervous-system activity, which is not the same as low mood.

If a learner assumes legal drugs are harmless, the reveal shows alcohol's liver damage and tobacco's lung cancer and cardiovascular harm: whether a drug is legal depends partly on history, culture and regulation, so being legal does not mean being safe.
activities.rationale: Attaching specific effects to specific organs and classifying drugs by nervous-system effect is a clear reveal-and-sort task; lift-the-flap predictions directly surface the common safety and classification misconceptions. A static authoritative illustration supports safeguarding-friendly, non-sensational delivery. The tap-to-reveal and flap interactions are suggested mechanisms to make the content concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Tap an organ on a body diagram to reveal the specific effect: liver → 'alcohol is broken down here; heavy use scars it (cirrhosis)'; lungs → 'tobacco smoke damages airways and causes cancer'; brain → 'depressants slow nerve signals, stimulants speed them up'; heart → tobacco's cardiovascular harm.
Use a side panel to sort each named drug (alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, a hallucinogen) into depressant / stimulant / hallucinogen by its nervous-system effect.

Open lift-the-flap myth-busters and predict the answer before revealing: 'Is alcohol a stimulant?' → 'No — it is a depressant that slows you down, which is why it impairs reactions.' / 'Can you be dependent without physical withdrawal?' → 'Yes — psychological dependence (craving) is real.'
activities.intendedInsight: A drug is a chemical that changes how a specific body system works. It can cause short-term changes in behaviour and, for some drugs (especially with heavy or long-term use), long-term organ damage. Effects vary with the drug, the dose and the person, so drugs are not simply 'good' or 'bad'.

activities.title: In-role conversation with a GP or addiction nurse
feedback: If a learner dismisses psychological dependence as 'not real' addiction, the responder distinguishes withdrawal-based physical dependence from craving/compulsion-based psychological dependence, noting both are powerful and real.
Responses should remain non-judgemental, safeguarding-aware and sensitive to pupils' personal contexts.
activities.rationale: A dialogue can ask open questions and probe a learner's reasoning on behaviour and dependence, which a static map does not; the body-map presents the defined organ-effects and classification content as a visual reveal, so these activities are complementary rather than ranked. Comparative efficacy of the dialogue format is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Ask an in-role GP or addiction nurse age-appropriate questions about how alcohol and tobacco affect the body, why dependence develops, and how to make safe choices.
Explain your own reasoning about a scenario (e.g. why someone might keep using a drug they know is harmful) and have it probed Socratically.
Work through why physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) differs from psychological dependence (craving, compulsion) in a real question-and-answer exchange.
activities.intendedInsight: Behaviour, decision-making and dependence can be explored through responsive dialogue that probes a learner's reasoning, complementing the factual organ-effect core.

activities.title: Classification and drug→organ check
feedback: For a wrong classification, re-anchor to the nervous-system effect: does the drug slow signals (depressant), speed them up (stimulant) or distort perception (hallucinogen)?
For a dependence item, remind: physical = body adapts and withdrawal appears; psychological = craving/compulsion.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and matching items check the factual core. These confirm recall and matching rather than eliciting independent explanation, so pair with the dialogue and body-map for reasoning.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Categorise named drugs as depressant, stimulant or hallucinogen.
Match each drug to the main organ(s) it harms (e.g. alcohol → liver/brain; tobacco → lungs/heart).
Answer items distinguishing physical from psychological dependence.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of the classification and specific organ harms, and of the physical/psychological dependence distinction.

activities.title: Optional reaction-time / synapse mini-model
feedback: If a learner expects alcohol to 'speed you up', the model shows a lengthened reaction time, reinforcing that a depressant slows signalling.
activities.rationale: A dynamic model can make the slow/speed mechanism concrete, but most of the syllabus is organ effects, classification and dependence, so this is a supporting option rather than the primary teach. It is a simplified illustration, not a measured physiological result.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Explore a simple model of nervous-system signal transmission where a depressant lengthens reaction time and a stimulant shortens it.
Compare the modelled reaction time for a depressant versus a stimulant and connect it to real behaviour (e.g. why alcohol impairs reactions).
activities.intendedInsight: Makes the mechanism felt: 'depressant' and 'stimulant' describe slowing or speeding of nervous-system signalling, which drives the behavioural effects.

constraints: Frame drugs mechanistically and non-judgementally — a chemical that changes how a body system works — not moralising.
Use accurate, age-appropriate, non-sensational information; attend to safeguarding and pupils' personal contexts.
Separate physical from psychological dependence explicitly, since learners routinely conflate them.
Connect effects to body systems already studied (nervous, circulatory, respiratory, liver) to consolidate prior learning.
Classification and matching items confirm recall and sorting; they do not by themselves elicit independent explanation of mechanism or dependence — pair with explanation/dialogue tasks.
The reaction-time model is a simplified representation of nervous-system signalling, not a measured physiological result.
This is UK-led (DfE KS3); there is no specific NGSS MS performance expectation, as US substance-effect content sits in health education.
No activity format is asserted as superior or necessary; medium choices are proposed affordances pending efficacy evidence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (BBC Bitesize KS3 claim) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its classification/organ-harm specifics as unverified secondary material.

Sources establish curriculum requirements and general classification/harm facts but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one activity format; relative 'best teach', 'faster' and 'efficient' judgements have been reduced to affordances.
Safeguarding: delivery must be adapted to the class context; the dialogue activity in particular needs a trusted, age-appropriate, non-sensational responder.

probeDeeper: If alcohol makes people feel confident, why does it actually slow reaction times and impair judgement?
Alcohol and tobacco are legal but heroin is not — does that ranking match how harmful they are? Why might law and harm not line up?
How is being physically dependent on a drug different from being psychologically dependent?
What specific long-term damage do alcohol and tobacco do to particular organs?
assess.correctAnswer: Alcohol is a depressant: it slows down the nervous system, giving slower reactions, impaired judgement and slurred speech, even though people feel less inhibited at first. 'Depressant' means it depresses (slows) nervous-system activity — not that it makes you sad. Being legal does not make it safe: alcohol causes liver damage and many deaths, and tobacco (also legal) causes lung cancer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Alcohol is a stimulant because it makes people lively and confident
errorPatterns.nextMove: The early 'confidence' comes from depressing self-control; overall alcohol slows the nervous system, so it's a depressant. Use reaction-time evidence.
errorPatterns.distractor: Alcohol is a stimulant — it gives you energy and confidence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies alcohol as a stimulant from the initial disinhibited feeling

errorPatterns.pattern: Legal drugs like alcohol and tobacco aren't really drugs or aren't dangerous
errorPatterns.nextMove: Alcohol and nicotine are drugs; legality reflects history and regulation, not safety. Both cause major, well-documented harm.
errorPatterns.distractor: Alcohol and tobacco aren't really drugs because they're legal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says only illegal substances are harmful drugs

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Depressant' means it makes you feel sad or depressed
errorPatterns.nextMove: In this context 'depressant' means it slows nervous-system activity; it is not the same as low mood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the everyday meaning of 'depressed' into the drug category

errorPatterns.pattern: You can't really get addicted without physical dependence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) from psychological dependence (craving, compulsion); both are powerful and real.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses psychological dependence as 'not real' addiction

responseLevels.gap: Classifies drugs by surface feelings and assumes legal means safe; can't define the categories.
responseLevels.full: Categorises drugs by their effect on the nervous system, argues that legality doesn't equal safety with organ-specific harms, and distinguishes physical from psychological dependence.
responseLevels.partial: Places some drugs in the right category and knows alcohol/tobacco are harmful, but slips on the depressant label or on separating legality from safety.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Alcohol is legal and is often described as a way to 'loosen up' and feel more confident, so some people assume it's a stimulant and basically harmless. Which category does alcohol actually belong to — depressant, stimulant, or hallucinogen — and does being legal make it safe? Explain what 'depressant' really means here.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the categories classifies by effect on the nervous system and separates legality from safety. A child who reasons from surface feelings calls alcohol a stimulant, or assumes 'legal' means 'not a dangerous drug'.
